source.title_on_document: Floor Raiser or Ceiling Limiter? Differential Storytelling Outcomes with a Child-Centric GenAI System Across Individual Differences

paper_design_summary: Secondary analysis of the school-based evaluation in Fan et al. (2025, StoryPrompt). Forty Chinese elementary children (Grades 2-6) each told one story with the StoryPrompt GenAI system (GPT-3.5 keywords, Stable Diffusion images) and one with a paper storyboard, in an order assigned at random to two counterbalanced groups. Five experts rated each story for creativity, richness, coherence, and narrative structure; quantitative analyses use the 38 children with both stories and focus on how the AI-minus-storyboard gain varies with baseline quality.

studies.label: Within-subjects school study (StoryPrompt vs paper storyboard)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of conditions (AI system first or storyboard first); every child did both conditions
assignment.quote: Children were randomly assigned to two counterbalanced order groups (Fig. 2).

arms.name: AI condition
arms.description: StoryPrompt: story planning, then six paragraphs each anchored by a GPT-3.5 keyword chosen from four strongly and four weakly associated options, with a Stable Diffusion comic image after each paragraph. Within-person condition; 18 children did it first.

arms.name: Storyboard condition
arms.description: Paper sheets with six slots, markers, and reference images; children sketched and wrote or dictated stories. Within-person condition; 20 children (of the 38 analyzed) did it first.

participants.exclusions: 40 children took part; the paper does not give a count at assignment. Two children (P36, P39) did not finish their storyboard stories because of time and were excluded from all quantitative analyses (N = 38); their AI-condition data were kept for qualitative analysis.
participants.who: Elementary school children aged 7-12 (Grades 2-6), 30 boys and 10 girls, from one public elementary school
participants.quote: Two participants (P36, Grade 3; P39, Grade 2) did not complete their storyboard stories due to time constraints ... P36 and P39 were excluded from all quantitative analyses ( N = 38 for all reported statistics).

ai_tool.name_model: StoryPrompt (authors' system; ChatGPT API GPT-3.5 for keywords, Stable Diffusion for images)
ai_tool.how_used: For each of six paragraphs the system offers eight GPT-3.5 keywords (four strongly, four weakly associated) that the child can pick and refresh; after each paragraph the child can generate and regenerate a comic-style image. Children compose all narrative text themselves, mainly by voice.

task.description: Oral and written storytelling: a six-paragraph story across three scenes, in Chinese
task.duration: 20-30 minutes per child in the AI condition; max 30 minutes per condition per Fig. 2

outcomes.name: Expert-rated creativity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Five experts used the Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT) to rate each story on creativity, richness, coherence, and narrative structure, each on a 1-to-5 scale. Raters were blind to condition but informed of the child’s grade; scores reflect grade-appropriate expectations, so grade-group comparisons are age-normed. Ratings were averaged across raters for each story and dimension (p. 10, Section 3.4).

contrasts.reported: No aggregate AI vs storyboard creativity means printed. Mean creativity gain (AI minus traditional), bottom third of baseline (N = 13): +1.292; top third (N = 13) overall composite gain -0.292 is not a creativity gain (the creativity bar is shown only in Fig. 4). Fig. 4 provides gain means and standard-error bars for all baseline terciles; these are subgroup results, and numerical standard errors are not printed. AI-condition creativity scores showed smaller dispersion, variance ratio = 2.27x (descriptive).
contrasts.locator: pp. 12-13, Section 4.1 and Fig. 4; p. 14, Section 4.1 and Fig. 7

outcomes.name: Composite story quality (mean of creativity, richness, coherence, narrative structure)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Five experts used the Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT) to rate each story on creativity, richness, coherence, and narrative structure, each on a 1-to-5 scale. Raters were blind to condition but informed of the child’s grade; scores reflect grade-appropriate expectations, so grade-group comparisons are age-normed. Ratings were averaged across raters for each story and dimension (p. 10, Section 3.4). Composite quality is the mean of the four dimension scores (p. 10, Section 3.4). Robustness checks of the baseline-linked convergence pattern used within-order correlations, cross-rater splits, and regression of AI-condition quality on traditional-condition quality (p. 12, Section 4.1).

contrasts.reported: 27 of 38 children showed positive composite-quality gains under AI while 11 showed negative gains. Gain by condition order: AI first N = 18, M = 0.21, SD = 0.80; traditional first N = 20, M = 0.32, SD = 0.52; Mann-Whitney U = 185.5, p = .884. These means, SDs, and Ns describe order groups, and the test compares gains between order groups, not overall AI-versus-storyboard arm levels. Fig. 4 provides composite gain means and standard-error bars by baseline tercile, with standard errors shown only graphically and no numerical standard errors printed. The median-split quality gap narrowed by 83.5%, from 1.028 (traditional) to 0.170 (AI); the paper labels this descriptive score compression, not an independent causal estimate.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 3.3; pp. 11-13, Section 4.1 and Fig. 4; p. 14, Section 4.1 and Fig. 7

outcomes.name: Expert-rated richness
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Five experts used the Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT) to rate each story on creativity, richness, coherence, and narrative structure, each on a 1-to-5 scale. Raters were blind to condition but informed of the child’s grade; scores reflect grade-appropriate expectations, so grade-group comparisons are age-normed. Ratings were averaged across raters for each story and dimension (p. 10, Section 3.4).

contrasts.reported: No aggregate AI vs storyboard richness means printed. Mean richness gain (AI minus traditional), bottom baseline tercile (N = 13): +1.369. Fig. 4 provides gain means and standard-error bars for all baseline terciles; these are subgroup results, and numerical standard errors are not printed. Age-normed richness, lower-grade vs higher-grade: AI M = 3.547 vs. 3.600, p = .883; traditional M = 2.726 vs. 3.205, p = .086. These p-values compare grade groups within each condition, not AI versus storyboard.
contrasts.locator: pp. 12-13, Section 4.1 and Fig. 4; p. 13, Section 4.1, Dimension-selective outcomes

outcomes.name: Expert-rated coherence
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Five experts used the Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT) to rate each story on creativity, richness, coherence, and narrative structure, each on a 1-to-5 scale. Raters were blind to condition but informed of the child’s grade; scores reflect grade-appropriate expectations, so grade-group comparisons are age-normed. Ratings were averaged across raters for each story and dimension (p. 10, Section 3.4).

contrasts.reported: No aggregate AI vs storyboard coherence means printed. In the top baseline tercile (N = 13), mean AI-minus-traditional coherence gain was -0.431. Fig. 4 shows gains for the lower baseline terciles and a decline for the top tercile, with gain means and standard-error bars by tercile. These are subgroup results, not an aggregate treatment estimate; numerical standard errors are not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Section 3.4; pp. 12-13, Section 4.1 and Fig. 4

outcomes.name: Expert-rated narrative structure
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Five experts used the Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT) to rate each story on creativity, richness, coherence, and narrative structure, each on a 1-to-5 scale. Raters were blind to condition but informed of the child’s grade; scores reflect grade-appropriate expectations, so grade-group comparisons are age-normed. Ratings were averaged across raters for each story and dimension (p. 10, Section 3.4).

contrasts.reported: No aggregate AI vs storyboard narrative-structure means printed. In the top baseline tercile (N = 13), mean AI-minus-traditional narrative-structure gain was -0.558. Fig. 4 shows gains for the lower baseline terciles and a decline for the top tercile, with gain means and standard-error bars by tercile; numerical standard errors are not printed. Under AI, lower-grade vs higher-grade age-normed narrative-structure ratings were M = 3.105 vs. 3.558, p = .010. This p-value compares grade groups within AI, not AI versus storyboard. These are subgroup results, not aggregate treatment estimates.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Section 3.4; pp. 12-13, Section 4.1 and Fig. 4; p. 13, Dimension-selective outcomes

outcomes.name: Text length (Chinese character count)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Text length is the Chinese character count of each story. Stories in both conditions were created and rated in Chinese, and all texts were reviewed against recorded audio for completeness (p. 10, Section 3.4). The paper does not state the counting procedure. No listed measure category exactly covers raw character count, so measure is null; no scoring model or lexical-overlap procedure is claimed.

contrasts.reported: Lower-grade vs higher-grade mean story length was 152 vs. 208 Chinese characters in the traditional condition and 240 vs. 259 in the AI condition. The printed p = .759 compares grade groups within AI, not AI versus traditional. Both grade groups had descriptively longer stories under AI; aggregate condition means, SDs, and an overall AI-versus-traditional test are not numerically reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Section 3.4; p. 13, Section 4.1, Text length and score compression

eligibility.reason: Within-person design with randomly assigned order (p. 9, Section 3.3), so criterion 1 is met, and creativity is rated by five blind experts (p. 10, Section 3.4). But only 38 children are analyzed (40 took part; p. 9, Section 3.2), below the 50-person threshold. List in the screening report as a small randomized experiment. The paper is a secondary analysis of the sample in Fan et al. (2025, StoryPrompt; p. 11, Section 3.5).

one_line_finding: With 38 children analyzed, the GenAI storytelling condition was associated with larger quality gains for children with low storyboard scores (baseline-gain rs = -0.730, p < .001; bottom-tercile creativity gain +1.292) and a median-split quality gap that narrowed by 83.5 percent (1.028 to 0.170), with no aggregate AI-versus-storyboard means printed (pp. 11-14).
